title: Campeau v. Yakima HMA, LLC
questions: In American Pipe and Construction Company v. Utah, the United States Supreme Court held that filing a class action tolls the running of the statute of limitations for all members of the class who make a timely motion to intervene after the class fails to certify. In a previous case, this court held that a nurses' association lacked associational standing to recover unpaid wages on behalf of its members. Daniel Campeau, a union nurse, filed this class action to recover unpaid wages. Campeau filed this case after the statute of limitations ran. This court must decide (1) whether Washington recognizes American Pipe tolling and (2) if so, whether that tolling rule applies to cases brought under a theory of associational standing

title: Envolve Pharmacy Sols., Inc. v. Dep't of Revenue
questions: Washington exempts "insurance business" from B&O tax on which a premiums tax "is paid." Do firms serving firms that pay premiums tax owe B&O tax?

title: Cousins v. Dep't of Corrections
questions: Is the plaintiff's action against the Department of Corrections for alleged violations of the Public Records Act barred by the one-year statute of limitations in RCW 42.56.550(6)? Does the discovery rule of accrual apply to the Public Records Act?

title: In re County, Attorney at Law
questions: Private landowners John Titcomb, Jr. and Linde Behringer object to the taking of a creek on their property by the City of Sammamish. Did the City have authority to condemn the creek as part of a larger project designed to manage stormwater and improve fish passage?

title: Greenberg v. Amazon.com, Inc.
questions: In March and April 2020, Alvin Greenberg and others purchased various goods from Amazon, which they needed to stay safe and healthy during the COVID-19 pandemic. However, the prices that they paid vastly exceeded pre-pandemic prices. They filed a lawsuit in federal court arguing that Amazon engaged in "price gouging," which is an unfair act or practice within the meaning of Washington's Consumer Protection Act. Amazon filed a motion to dismiss the lawsuit. The federal court now asks this court the following questions: (1) Is "price gouging" an unfair act or practice within the meaning of Washington's Consumer Protection Act? (2) If so, does the court or the jury decide when a claim of "price gouging" is unfair?

title: Spokane County v. Meneses
questions: The Washington State Department of Social and Health Services (DSHS) provides competency related services to persons facing criminal charges in the state. Spokane County Prosecuting Attorney Lawrence Haskell filed an original action in this court, seeking a writ of mandamus ordering Secretary of DSHS Jilma Meneses to timely provide competency evaluations and restoration treatment for certain criminal defendants charged with felony offenses in Spokane County. Is the Secretary of DSHS a state officer under the Washington Constitution? Is a writ of mandamus appropriate to compel the Secretary to timely provide competency services to criminal defendants?

title: AURC III, LLC v. Point Ruston Phase II, LLC
questions: Whether payment of an arbitration award renders a case moot; may a court attach an arbitrator's reasoning to an order?

title: Benton County Water Conservancy Bd. v. Dep't of Ecology
questions: The Benton County Water Conservancy Board seeks judicial review of the Department of Ecology's processing of certain water right transfer applications. Does the Board have standing under the Administrative Procedure Act to do so?

title: Gardens Condo. v. Farmers Ins. Exch.
questions: Gardens sought coverage under its insurance policy, issued by Farmers, for damage to the roof of its condominium building. The damage stemmed from faulty workmanship, which caused condensation and water vapor to accumulate. The policy did not cover damage from faulty workmanship nor damage in the "sequence of events" following faulty workmanship. However, the faulty workmanship exclusion had a "resulting loss exception" that preserved coverage for damage that was otherwise covered by the policy. Does the insurance policy's resulting loss exception preserve coverage for resulting loss even if it occurs in the chain of events following an excluded event?

title: Assoc. Gen. Contractors of Wash. v. State
questions: Under the Prevailing Wage for Public Works Act, chapter 39.12 RCW, employers must pay workers on public works projects no less than the prevailing wage for such work in the area. The industrial statistician is responsible for determining those prevailing wages. Before 2018, the statistician usually determined prevailing wages by using wage surveys. In 2018, the legislature directed the industrial statistician to base the prevailing wage on collective bargaining agreements when applicable. SSB 5493 (2018). A law violates our state constitution if it renders erroneous a straightforward determination of the scope of rights or duties under a preexisting law without setting the preexisting law forth in full. CONST. art. II, § 37. Does SSB 5493 render erroneous a straightforward determination of rights or duties under RCW 39.12.026?

title: State v. Luthi
questions: The Cowlitz County Jail courtroom routinely uses an in-court holding cell for nonjury hearings. Is this in- court holding cell an inherently prejudicial restraint which requires an individualized inquiry into its use before each court appearance?

title: Spencer v. Franklin Hills Health-Spokane, LLC
questions: In a lawsuit against a corporation, service of process must be delivered to a person in a role specified under RCW 4.28.080(9), such as the head of the corporation, the corporation's registered agent, the corporation's managing agent, or an office assistant to one of those people. In this case, a human resources and payroll manager received the documents. Was service properly accomplished under the statute?

title: Suarez v. State
questions: Under the Washington Laws Against Discrimination, an employer has a duty to reasonably accommodate the religious practices of their employees unless doing so would cause an "undue hardship" for the employer. Suarez's former employer seeks review of the Court of Appeals' analysis of their "undue hardship" defense

title: State v. Kelly
questions: Is Kelly entitled to resentencing after Blake rendered the offender scores used for his original sentencings incorrect?

title: State v. Vasquez
questions: Vasquez was convicted of first degree murder that he committed when he was 23. Years later, he filed a CrR 7.8 motion asserting that Blake required a reduction in his offender score. He was resentenced, but the court refused to hear arguments. Does the grant of a CrR 7.8 motion to vacate and resentence give the resentencing court the discretion to consider all sentencing issues? Does the court have the discretion to limit the parties' arguments?

title: State v. McGee
questions: On June 3, 2017, police illegally detained Malcolm McGee in the course of a narcotics investigation and recorded their findings in a law enforcement database. When an associate of McGee was later found dead, homicide investigators used the illegally-obtained information in the June 3 report to obtain search warrants targeting McGee. We must now resolve whether Washington's attenuation doctrine allows the State to use unlawfully obtained evidence-here, the information obtained during the narcotics investigation and evidence later derived from it-when an independent and unforeseeable act makes that evidence relevant to the investigation of a different crime

title: In re Wallstrom, Attorney at Law
In re Marriage of Wilcox
questions: A 1968 Washington Supreme Court case suggests that spousal maintenance awards are only appropriate when a requesting spouse needs it. In 1973, the legislature amended relevant statutes on the subject. Does a trial court abuse its discretion under RCW 26.09.090 when it orders a spousal maintenance award in an amount and duration that exceeds the requesting spouse's needs?

title: State v. Smith
questions: Every person accused of a crime has the right to be tried by an impartial jury of their peers who will presume them innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt. When a potential juror makes statements that suggests they have prejudged some aspect of the case and the trial court finds they cannot put aside their opinions and try the case impartially, the judge must remove the juror. Smith alleges that a biased juror was permitted to sit on his jury, thereby depriving him of his right to a fair trial and entitling him to a new trial. Appellate courts review challenges such as this for abuse of discretion. The court must decide whether, based on the juror's questionnaire responses and statements made during voir dire, there was a clear probability of juror bias such that no reasonable judge could have found the juror was able to set aside their biases and try the case impartially

title: Antio, LLC v. Dep't of Rev.
questions: Businesses may deduct "amounts derived from investments" from their B&O tax obligations. This court previously defined "investments" in the statute to mean "incidental investments of surplus funds." The legislature then revised the statute in response to a Washington Supreme Court decision on a different issue. Did this revision do away with the court's earlier definition of investments and allow businesses to deduct more than "incidental investments of surplus funds"?

title: King County v. Friends of Sammamish Valley
questions: King County recently passed Ordinance 19030, liberalizing regulations pertaining to wineries, breweries, and distilleries on agricultural land. Does the Ordinance violate the Growth Management Act's protection of agricultural land? Did the County conduct an adequate environmental review under the State Environmental Policy Act?

title: In re Dependency of A.H.
questions: Does a statute bar appeals in juvenile cases absent specific direction from client? Must a lawyer prove such direction?

title: In re Dependency of Baby Boy B.
questions: Shelter care is temporary physical care in a licensed facility or in a home. RCW 13.34.030(24). Under certain circumstances, a child may be removed from their parents and placed in shelter care. Ch. 13.34 RCW. Under Washington law, "[n]o child may be placed in shelter care for longer than thirty days without an order, signed by the judge, authorizing continued shelter care." RCW 13.34.065(7)(a)(i). In this case, a superior court declined to hold monthly shelter care review hearings. This court must decide whether RCW 13.34.065(7)(a)(i) requires monthly hearings

title: In re Disciplinary Proc. Against Huynh
questions: In this attorney discipline proceeding, Huynh was charged with theft, false representation, and other misconduct. The hearing officer recommended disbarment and the Washington State Bar Association Disciplinary Board unanimously affirmed. Should we uphold the hearing officer's findings of fact and conclusions of law in light of Huynh's challenges for lack of substantial evidence and due process violations? Should Huynh be disbarred?

title: In re Pers. Restraint of Frazier
questions: Charles Frazier seeks resentencing for crimes he committed when he was 18 years old. He argues that his personal restraint petition is not time barred because scientific studies regarding late adolescent brain development is newly discovered evidence that was not available when he was sentenced in 1989. Does the newly discovered evidence exception for collateral attacks apply to sentencings?

title: City of Tacoma v. Dep't of Ecology
questions: The Department of Ecology, in a denial letter, committed to limiting nitrogen discharges into Puget Sound through their "individual permitting process." Subsequently, Ecology issued two individual permits and a general permit for wastewater treatment plants that limited nitrogen discharges. This court must decide whether Ecology's denial letter created a "rule" without going through the Administrative Procedure Act's rulemaking process

title: U.S. Sportsmen’s All. Found. v. Smith
questions: Washington Fish and Wildlife (WFW) Commissioner Lorna Smith simultaneously held a position on the Jefferson County Planning Commission. RCW 77.04.040 prohibits WFW commissioners from holding "another state, county, or municipal elective or appointive office." We are asked to determine whether a county planning commission position is an "office" under the statute

title: In re Disciplinary Proc. Against Monro
questions: Stephen Kenneth Monro is a Washington attorney currently facing discipline related to converting client funds. After an evidentiary hearing, the hearing officer recommended disbarment. The Discipline Board remanded the matter to the hearing officer to clarify unspecified findings and conclusions and to conduct a proportionality review. This case asks us to determine whether the Board had the authority to order this remand and, if so, whether that authority was properly exercised here

title: In re Kelley, Attorney at Law
questions: Should the Supreme Court adopt the WSBA Disciplinary Board's recommendation for disbarment?

title: In re Dependency of M.L.W.
questions: Does mother have standing to assert child's right to intervene where child had attorney below? Did DCYF prove it offered all necessary services capable of correcting mother's parental deficiencies within foreseeable future?

title: State v. Richards
questions: Richards failed to restrain her dangerous dog when it was outside of its proper enclosure, a violation of a Wahkiakum County ordinance. The district court imposed a jail term of 364 days for this gross misdemeanor, but it conditioned the suspension of the jail term on Richards surrendering the dog to the animal control authority. Did the court exceed its sentencing authority by imposing this condition on the suspended sentence?

title: In re Dependency of Z.A.
questions: Three children were found dependent, meaning that they did not have parents or guardians capable of taking care of them. In such circumstances, a judge can order the children placed out of their homes only if (among other things) the court finds: (a) There is no parent or guardian available to care for such child; (b) The parent, guardian, or legal custodian is not willing to take custody of the child; or (c) The court finds, by clear, cogent, and convincing evidence, a manifest danger exists that the child will suffer serious abuse or neglect if the child is not removed from the home. RCW 13.34.130(6). The State argued, and the trial court agreed, that the father was not "available" because he could not provide adequate care for the children. Was that the right standard to apply?

title: In re Individual, Attorney at Law
questions: Was the plaintiff's late-filed complaint "constructively filed" in a timely manner?

title: John Does 1, 2, 4, & 5 v. Seattle Police Dep't
questions: Public records requests were made regarding the activities of Seattle police officers on January 6, 2021. Are the officers entitled to a preliminary injunction preventing disclosure of the public records? Can they litigate under pseudonym? What is an agency's obligation when disclosure may implicate a third party's constitutional rights?

title: In re Marriage of Porter
questions: A military officer and his former spouse began drawing monthly military retirement benefits divided in their divorce. Several years after his retirement, the officer is involuntarily recalled to active duty service. During the recall to active duty, the officer is promoted and later retires with a higher rank and increased pension benefits. Is the former spouse entitled to a share of the increased pension accrued during the involuntary recalled service? If so, does federal law prohibit state courts from including increased pension benefits earned during involuntary service as community property?

title: State v. Olsen
questions: In State v. Blake (2021), this court declared Washington's drug possession statute unconstitutional. Prior to Blake, Christopher Olsen pleaded guilty to multiple charges, including drug possession. Is Olsen entitled to withdraw his guilty pleas to all the charges in light of Blake?

title: State v. Willyard
questions: In 2003, Nicole Willyard pleaded guilty to obstruction, unlawful possession of a controlled substance, and bail jumping. In 2021, this court decided State v. Blake, which invalidated Washington's former unlawful possession of a controlled substance statute. In response, Willyard moved to withdraw her guilty pleas. The superior court has already vacated her possession charge. This court must now decide whether Willyard is also entitled to withdraw her guilty plea to unlawful possession or the other associated offenses.

title: State v. Harris
questions: Does Houston-Sconiers require consideration of youth in plea agreements and joint sentencing recommendations?

title: Brown v. Old Navy, LLC
questions: The Washington Commercial Electronic Mail Act (CEMA) prohibits the sending of commercial emails that "contain[] false or misleading information in the subject line." This case asks us to determine whether the statute prohibits the transmission of a commercial email with a subject line containing any false or misleading information, or if it only prohibits subject lines that conceal the email's commercial nature

title: State v. J.H.-M.
questions: Is a custody condition prohibiting "sexually explicit conduct" defined by RCW 9.68A.011(4) unconstitutionally vague?

title: Atkerson v. Dep’t of Child., Youth, & Fams.
questions: A child received a fatal injury a few weeks after the State opened a child abuse investigation. Washington State has immunized itself and its agents for "acts or omissions in emergent placement investigations of child abuse . . . unless the act or omission constitutes gross negligence. Emergent placement investigations are those conducted prior to a shelter care hearing under RCW 13.34.065." RCW 4.24.595. This immunity "include[s], but [is] not limited to, any determination to leave a child with a parent . . . or to return a child to a parent." RCW 4.24.595. The court must decide whether this immunity applied in this case. The court must also decide whether the trial court erred in excluding one of the State's expert witnesses, a retired trial judge

title: State v. Morgan
questions: A trial court generally has broad discretion when imposing restitution. However, when a victim is paid benefits under the Crime Victims' Compensation Act (CVCA), RCW 9.94.753(7) requires a court to order restitution. Does RCW 9.94A.753 allow a trial court discretion to modify the amount of restitution when ordered for benefits paid under the CVCA?

title: Jewels Helping Hands v. Hansen
questions: Are orders on pre-election initiative challenges reviewable? Is this local initiative within the local initiative power?

title: Raab v. Nu Skin Enters., Inc.
questions: Some contracts include a clause that pre-selects a location, or "forum," for resolving future disputes relating to the contract. How does a party seek enforcement of this contractual "forum-selection clause"? What is the proper scope of the court's analysis?

title: David v. Freedom Vans LLC
questions: RCW 49.62.070 addresses the extent of an employer's authority to restrict low wage employees from accepting outside employment. Employer Freedom Vans required employees David and Springer to sign a noncompete agreement restricting them from directly or indirectly engaging in any business that competed with Freedom Vans. Does Freedom Vans's noncompete agreement violate RCW 49.62.070?

title: Thurman v. Cowles Co.
questions: Does Washington's new anti-SLAPP law, the Uniform Public Expression Act, apply to a defamation claim filed before the Act's effective date but later amended? Does the Uniform Public Expression Act violate the right of access to courts, the right of administration of justice without delay, and the privileges and immunities provision of our constitutions?

title: Hall v. Walgreens Boots All., Inc.
questions: Under RCW 19.86.170, is labeling as "non-drowsy" an over-the-counter antitussive containing dextromethorphan hydrobromide an "action[] . . . permitted by . . . [a] regulatory body . . . acting under statutory authority . . . of . . . the United States" such that this labeling decision falls within the statutory safe harbor?

title: State v. Mercedes
questions: In this case, animal control officers went to Ms. Mercedes' property to investigate two separate complaints of animal starvation and neglect made by the next-door neighbor. The officers did not have a search warrant. When the officers arrived at the property, they asked Ms. Mercedes to see the animals, which were inside a fenced pasture, and she agreed. Observations gathered while at her property were used to secure a search warrant of the property which led to charges of animal cruelty against Ms. Mercedes. The trial court granted Ms. Mercedes' motion to suppress the evidence and the Court of Appeals reversed. Ms. Mercedes argues that her consent to let the officers see the animals in her pasture was invalid because the officers did not warn her that she could refuse, limit, or later revoke that consent-referred to as Ferrier warnings. Her argument is based on our caselaw that requires law enforcement officers without a search warrant to provide Ferrier warnings when seeking permission to search a person's home for contraband or evidence of a crime. The issue here is whether the officers were required to give Ferrier warnings when they requested permission to search Ms. Mercedes' outdoor property

title: City of Wenatchee v. Stearns
questions: Frank Stearns was pulled over for DUI after a citizen's 911 call, an officer's brief contact with the caller on the scene, and the officer's observations of Stearns's driving. Did the officer have reasonable suspicion? 11:00 AM

title: Pub. Util. Dist. No. 1 of Snohomish County v. State
questions: Barry Chrisman was seriously injured when a tree blew down in a windstorm and fell onto his car. The area around the accident site had been recently logged, except for a band of trees in a Riparian Management Zone that were required to be left standing for environmental benefit. The Forest Practices Act immunizes forestland owners when trees required to be left standing in riparian areas blow down and cause damage or injury. Does the Forest Practices Act immunize the defendants in this case? Is immunity dependent on whether the Riparian Management Zone was accurately drawn?

title: In re Styles, Attorney at Law
State v. Zghair
questions: A jury convicted Zghair for felony murder by second degree assault. Was the evidence sufficient to prove he either committed the shooting as the principal or was an accomplice?

title: Vet Voice Found. v. Hobbs
questions: Washington voters who cast their votes by mail must sign a ballot declaration swearing that they are qualified to vote and have not already voted in the election. Election workers are in turn required to "verify that the voter's signature on the ballot declaration is the same as the signature of that voter in the registration files of the county." RCW 29A.40.110(3). If election workers cannot verify the voter's signature matches one of the signatures on file, they must attempt to contact the voter and give them an opportunity to cure. If the voter does not cure the defect, the ballot is disqualified and will not be counted. Signature verification disproportionally disqualifies the ballots of young people and people of color, among others. Vet Voice and other groups have sued the state, arguing that signature verification facially violates the due process, privileges and immunities, and freedom of elections clauses of our state constitution. The court is asked to decide the proper level of scrutiny that applies to this constitutional challenge and, under that proper scrutiny, whether signature verification is unconstitutional

title: M.R. v. State
questions: Does Washington's special statute of limitations for bringing claims that stem from injuries suffered as a result of childhood sexual abuse preclude claims of continuing sexual abuse by the same perpetrator that begin at childhood and extend into the victim's adulthood?

title: State v. Lewis
questions: Under the Sentencing Reform Act, judges make sentencing decisions based in part on the defendant's "offender score." The offender score is determined by counting "points" for each of the defendant's previous convictions, based on a set of rules under RCW 9.94A.525. At issue in this case is RCW 9.94A.525(3), which says that "out-of- state" convictions can be counted in the offender score. For the purpose of the offender score calculation, do convictions from foreign countries count as "out-of-state" convictions?

title: State v. Nelson
questions: Jasper Nelson brings a preenforcement challenge to community custody conditions requiring random breath and urinalysis testing to monitor his compliance with valid conditions prohibiting alcohol and drug use. Nelson argues the testing conditions are unconstitutional because his underlying offenses did not involve alcohol or drugs. Should the court strike the testing conditions?

title: Cockrum v. C.H. Murphy/Clark-Ullman, Inc.
questions: An employee may sue their employer for workplace injuries under RCW 51.24.020 only if the employer deliberately intended the injury. Are there genuine issues of material fact that Cockrum's employer deliberately intended to cause his mesothelioma?

title: Hous. Auth. v. Knight
questions: Does the CARES Act require 30 days' notice for all evictions or only for nonpayment of rent?

title: State v. J.M.H.
questions: JuCR 7.16 & RCW 13.40.040 address juvenile warrants. Is JuCr 7.16 constitutional? Was this warrant order appealable?
